'''''Pandanus furcatus''''' (common name '''Pandan Atono''') [[Roxb.]], also known as korr, pandan or Himalayan/Nepal screw pine (named for the screw-like [[phyllotaxy|arrangement of its leaves]]), is native to the [[Sikkim]] [[Himalaya]] of Northeast [[India]], [[Bhutan]] and [[Nepal]], [[Malaysia]], [[Indonesia]] and [[West Africa]], and occurs on moist and shady slopes of ravines between 300 and 1500 m. As might be expected it is cold-resistant and able to tolerate occasional light frost, slowly growing to a tall branched tree, about 17 m at maturity, and perched on stilt-like aerial roots. The crown is made up of [[linear]] leaves 5 m long, pale-green, with finely toothed margins, rarely up to 6 m long (exceeded in the genus only by ''[[Pandanus laxespicatus]]'').<ref>{{cite book | last= Everett | first= Thomas H. | date= 1968 | title= Living Trees of the World | location= New York | publisher= Doubleday and Co.| page= 68}}</ref> The leathery flower [[spathe]]s are golden-yellow, the lowermost are largest and about 1m in length. These give rise to cone-like fruit, 15–25 cm long, that are bright orange to red when mature and consist of numerous 5-6 angled drupes; they are edible and sweet-tasting.

This species was first described by [[William Roxburgh]] in 1814 in ''Hortus Bengalensis'', from a specimen growing in the [[East India Company]]'s Botanical Garden at [[Calcutta]]. Some two centuries later it has become a popular plant in cold climate gardens, though it is also cultivated throughout the tropics and subtropics. The tree from which the colour plate was made by [[Matilda Smith]], was acquired in 1888 by [[Royal Botanic Gardens, Kew|Kew]] from a [[Ghent]] nurseryman, who believed it to have originated from [[Madagascar]].<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://www.botanicus.org/page/471481|title=Botanicus.org: Curtis's botanical magazine.|website=www.botanicus.org|access-date=2018-03-21}}</ref> Besides the Himalayan region, the species also occurs naturally in [[China]] in [[Guangxi]], [[Xizang]] and [[Yunnan]], also in [[Myanmar]] and in [[Java]], [[Sumatra]] and [[Malaysia]].<ref>{{GRIN | accessdate = 25 January 2018}}</ref>

==Ethnobotany==
[[Lepet]] prepared specially for [[Eid al-Fitr]] in [[Jakarta]] is wrapped in the leaves, which are locally known as ''jelutuk''.<ref>{{cite journal|doi=10.1186/s42779-023-00197-0 |doi-access=free |title="Lepet": Indonesian traditional food for Eid Al-Fitr celebrations |date=2023 |last1=Wardana |first1=Ata Aditya |last2=Setiarto |first2=R. Haryo Bimo |last3=Wigati |first3=Laras Putri |journal=Journal of Ethnic Foods |volume=10 |article-number=29 }}</ref> [[Malays (ethnic group)|Malays]] in the Meliau subdistrict call the plant ''ledang'' and use it for wrapping food.<ref>{{cite journal|doi= 10.23887/jppp.v7i2.64370|title= An Ethnobotany-Based on Wrapping Plant of Malays Tribe in Meliau Subdistrict|date= 2023|last1= Sabilla|first1= Sabilla Narulita|last2= Sunandar|first2= Ari|last3= Setiadi|first3= Anandita Eka|journal= Jurnal Penelitian Dan Pengembangan Pendidikan|volume= 7|issue= 2|pages= 254–263|s2cid= 260650450|doi-access= free}}</ref> The fruit and seeds are eaten across much of its range as a food or medicine, while the roots are eaten for medicinal value.<ref>{{cite journal|url=https://www.phytojournal.com/archives?year=2016&vol=5&issue=3&ArticleId=850|last1= Singh|first1=Gurmeet|last2= Parle|first2=Amrita|title=Unique pandanus - Flavour, food and medicine|journal=Journal of Pharmacognosy and Phytochemistry|date= 2016|volume= 5|issue= 3|pages= 08–14}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|url=http://db.kib.ac.cn/CNFlora/SearchResult.aspx?cpni=CPNI-036-03309 | title=详细内容 }}</ref> Extracts from the leaves, stems and roots are used in India to treat [[dysentery]].<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Hadi|first1=Surya|last2=Bremner|first2=John B.|date=2001-01-16|title=Initial Studies on Alkaloids from Lombok Medicinal Plants|journal=Molecules|language=en|volume=6|issue=2|pages=117–129|doi=10.3390/60100117|doi-access=free}}</ref>

The [[Serampas]] people of [[Sumatra]] call the plant ''pandan singkil'', and cultivate it near dwellings to ward off malevolent spirits.<ref>{{cite journal |last1= Hariyadi |first1=B. |last2= Ticktin |first2=T. |date=2012-04-16 |title=Uras: Medicinal and Ritual Plants of Serampas, Jambi Indonesia
 |url=https://ethnobotanyjournal.org/era/index.php/era/article/view/673 |journal=Ethnobotany Research and Applications |volume=10 |issue=2012 |pages=133–149 |doi=10.17348/era.10.0.133-149 |access-date=2023-09-30|doi-access=free |hdl=10125/23551 |hdl-access=free }}</ref> 

In many parts of its range, the plant is used to make mats or for other weaving,<ref>{{cite book|doi=10.1007/978-981-33-4654-3|title=Tropical Peatland Eco-management|date=2021 |isbn=978-981-33-4653-6 |s2cid=233187955 |editor-last1=Osaki |editor-last2=Tsuji |editor-last3=Foead |editor-last4=Rieley |editor-first1=Mitsuru |editor-first2=Nobuyuki |editor-first3=Nazir |editor-first4=Jack }}</ref> and usage in China (where the synonym [[Pandanus urophyllus]] is commonly used) as a textile or fibrous weaving material extends to use in roofing, as well as in a variety of cultural applications. ''Pandanus'' leaves are used for weaving pandan mats, ropes, house-building materials, hats and carrying bags. Among the [[Orang Rimba people]], the plant is called ''Mengkuang ladang'', and its textile use extends to the production of ''sumpit'' cases which hold tobacco or cigarettes.<ref>{{cite journal|doi=10.14203/beritabiologi.v14i2.1816|doi-broken-date=12 July 2025 |url=https://e-journal.biologi.lipi.go.id/index.php/berita_biologi/article/view/1816/0 |title=Etnobotani Pandan (Pandanaceae) di Taman Nasional Bukit Duabelas, Jambi |journal=Berita Biologi |date=2015 |volume=14 |issue=2 |pages=121–129 |last1=Prasaja |first1=Dimas |last2=Muhadiono |first2=Muhadiono |last3=Hilwan |first3=Iwan }}</ref> Its cultivation for textile use is reported in parts of its range where fruiting does not occur, where it may be called ''iro'ut'' or ''pandan kowang'' in Indonesia's [[East Seram Regency]].<ref>{{cite journal|doi=10.1088/1755-1315/883/1/012009 |title=Species of pandan (Pandanus sp) in Gorom Island, East Seram Regency |date=2021 |last1=Sahupala |first1=A. |last2=Siahaya |first2=T. E. |last3=Seipala |first3=B. B. |last4=Siahaya |first4=L. |last5=Pelupessy |first5=L. |last6=Komul |first6=Y.D. |journal=IOP Conference Series: Earth and Environmental Science |volume=883 |issue=1 |article-number=012009 |bibcode=2021E&ES..883a2009S |s2cid=240226128 |doi-access=free }}</ref>

Known as Cangkuang in the [[Sundanese language]], it is also used for ritual uses, in which context, it lends its name to the temple [[Cangkuang]].<ref>{{cite journal|doi=10.13057/biodiv/d100308 |title=Ethnobotanical study on the Genus Pandanus L. F. In certain areas in Java, Indonesia |date=2009 |last1=Wardah |first1=Wardah |last2=Setyowati |first2=Francisca Murti |journal=Biodiversitas Journal of Biological Diversity |volume=10 |issue=3 |doi-access=free }}</ref>
